title: Regression: Intercept, Slope and Least Squares
summary: Thirty generated observations and a line the learner moves by hand. Every residual is drawn, optionally as the literal square whose area is being minimised, and the sum of squared errors updates live against a goal banner; a reveal then shows the least-squares solution, which no amount of dragging beats. The region outside the observed range of x is shaded, so the intercept can be seen to be a prediction for somebody who does not exist, and a disclosure shows the identical fit with x centred on its mean - same slope, same predictions, same residuals, and an intercept that finally describes a real part of the data. The challenge asks for one interpolated prediction, one extrapolated one, and a decision about which to report.
learningObjectives: Define a residual as an observation minus a prediction.
Explain what the least-squares criterion minimises and why no other line can do better.
Interpret a slope and an intercept in the units of the study.
Explain when an intercept is mathematically necessary and substantively empty, and what centring does about it.
Distinguish interpolation from extrapolation and say what R squared does and does not tell you.
interactionTypes: hand-fitting a line against a live error total
numeric prediction challenge with a judgement
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the dataset is generated in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, checkboxes, radio groups, number inputs and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; the two sliders announce their values in the units of the study, such as 'a slope of 0.68 points per extra minute of practice'. The chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired inside its figure with a visible three-column table setting the candidate line's intercept, slope, error total and variance accounted for beside the least-squares values once revealed, and a disclosure holds a six-row comparison of the raw and mean-centred parameterisations. The candidate line is solid and the revealed line dashed, both are named at their right-hand ends, the region with no data is hatched as well as tinted and labelled 'no data', and the goal checklist writes '(met)' or '(not yet)' in words. Negative variance accounted for is reported as 'none - worse than the mean' rather than clamped. The pinned primary result measures 517px tall at 1366x768. Every action announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to the laboratory and challenge headings as they open, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: Try to beat the least-squares line, then find out what the intercept is a prediction for
simulationNotes: Thirty observations are generated from a seeded generator: x is uniform between 12 and 68 minutes and y is 30 plus 0.6 times x plus normal noise with a standard deviation of 7. The least-squares solution is written down directly - the slope is the covariance of x and y over the variance of x, the intercept is whatever puts the line through the point of means - rather than searched for, so the reveal is an answer and not a better guess. At seed 2884 the fitted line is a predicted score of 27.7 plus 0.68 times minutes, with a squared error total of 1399 and 71.5 per cent of the variance accounted for; the mean of x is 35.9 minutes and the mean of y is 52.3 points, so the mean-centred parameterisation has the same slope, the same predictions of 48.2 at thirty minutes and 65.3 at fifty-five, the same error total, and an intercept of 52.3 instead of 27.7. R squared is reported for the candidate line as well and is allowed to go negative, because a line worse than predicting the mean of y for everybody is exactly what a negative value means. No standard errors or confidence intervals are computed, and the assumptions behind least squares are not checked - that is the following tool in this module. Nothing here is real data, and the slope is a comparison between people rather than a statement about changing anybody.
